utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon. Mr. Oric, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to my learned friends of the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel Ms. Patricia Sellers and case manager Donnica Henry-Frijlink, and later on after the break, Ms. Joanne Richardson will take my place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and I appear together with Mr. John Jones as Defence counsel for Mr. Naser Oric. With us today are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. We promised you a decision on the oral motion made yesterday by the Prosecution in relation to the recalling of Witness Eric. We have discussed it amongst ourselves and came to the conclusion -- and come to the conclusion that on the basis of the same arguments which were used in our written decision to -- now a decision to grant the recall -- the Defence motion for the recall of the witness, we feel that it is only just -- that the same circumstances apply to the Prosecution, who will be, therefore, authorised to examine in chief also the witness, but solely on matters which arise out of the video and on nothing else. In other words, it doesn't mean that the direct examination is reopened for all intents and purposes. It's being made very clear. We had the choice between just re-examination, but that, in our opinion, wouldn't have been fair, because the rediscovery of this video opens wide some issues which you are both entitled to explore, one on direct, the other one on cross. So that's our decision. Are there any preliminaries before we proceed? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one matter, Your Honour, and it concerns the second of today's witnesses. I can mention his name, because he doesn't enjoy protective measures. It's Slavoljub Filipovic. We discussed last Friday non-disclosure issues relating specifically to Mr. Filipovic. Your Honours may recall there was a discussion about a document which was shown to Ms. Trifunovic, and in that regard, I had passed up to Your Honours a chronology and some documents attached thereto, which Your Honours may still have. And among those papers, you saw that there was the name Filipovic and a list of documents which we had requested from the Prosecution but not received. Indeed, there are even three documents relating to Slavoljub Rankic, who is testifying today, which we hadn't received. Yesterday we received a box, and it's here as a visual aid, of material relating to Slavoljub Filipovic, and it was disclosed as potential exhibits to be used by the Prosecution with that witness initially as opposed to meeting our request for those documents which dates back to July of this year. Then subsequently, we were informed that those wouldn't be used as exhibits. The basic point is that we obviously have not had time to review that material in time for today's witness, and so if there is material there which is significant, we're going to be faced with an issue of recall or some other remedy for that extremely belated disclosure. That's one issue. The second issue relates to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you move to the next one. Does the same argument apply also to the next issue, the one that was due on Friday? I'm not going to mention his name, because I don't recall -- it's the one on Friday, anyway. You should have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of the witness for Friday. I'm just looking at our letter again. Yes, there are indeed documents relating to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in other words, we can't switch getting the one on Friday. Yes, but it doesn't work in any case because he probably still needs to be briefed or whatever, I don't know. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Our position is we're prepared to go ahead and cross-examine these witnesses, but we do protest at this practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're perfectly right to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Also, as regards proofing notes, we were told that we wouldn't receive proofing notes for Mr. Filipovic, but then one hour before today's hearing, we were told that there were proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That happens. And that's not going to cause an earthquake. That happens in the case of many, or most witnesses, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's really a question of when dramatically new information is revealed by those notes which we then have to pursue in the field. So I raise those two points, Your Honour, as a preliminary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I see it, I honestly don't think we are going to finish with the next witness, with Filipovic, today. I find it very difficult to anticipate that we would finish with that witness today, which would bring us to tomorrow. And by tomorrow, maybe you would have solved the problem. So what I suggest is that you start today, then you have the rest of the evening, or what will be left of it, and tomorrow morning to go through that mass of documents, if you can, but I suppose it shouldn't be difficult for you to sift the chaff from the wheat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. That's the course we intended to pursue. It seemed appropriate to raise it with Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But I appreciate very much the fact that you have raised it, in fact, and I am going to call on the Prosecution for an explanation of this. Because this has happened in the past, obviously, but -- and it will continue happening. But the unfortunate thing is when it happens, the day, the same day the witness is going to give evidence or the day before the witness is going to give evidence, because it becomes impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who is going to address this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me first state that I would be pleased, out of courtesy, if I receive a call from Defence in advance or just before the trial, so I can prepare and not check that while you are -- or Your Honours or Defence counsel is pleading it. It's so easy to update me. In the meanwhile, we did some checks, and we are happy to inform you later on when we in fact disclosed the material in an earlier stage. It's sometimes, Your Honour, that we receive a bundle of documents with a content of, let's say, 10 or 12 statements by a court, a municipal court in Bosnia, let's say, and that we translate these documents and that we disclose these documents as indeed a bundle, a compilation of it. And then later on, as a courtesy, as a confirmation, we do specific during certain stage of trial when we come to it again the disclosure, but then the particular statement itself. So there's a double disclosure. I cannot tell you now off the top of my head if we disclosed all of these statements, but at least a chunk of it, or even most of it, have already been disclosed through the rules of the road file on October -- from October the 3rd, and these were indeed disclosed under these rules of the road, where we trace those bundle of statements. So we will check further out, and we would like to inform you further on. And again, I offer, when -- out of a courtesy call, this can do, before the trial start on the particular day, or just to give me a call in that respect, I can more easily reflect in a quick manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What surprises me is what I consider an act of discourtesy on the part of the Prosecution in providing a box full of documents the day before the witness is supposed to come here and give evidence, as being documents that maybe - maybe - you know, you never know, maybe the Prosecution could use in the course of the examination-in-chief. All of a sudden it's inverted and you are expecting courtesy from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No. It is not for me that the Prosecution claims that they're acting in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can tell you, Mr. Wubben, I'm going to interrupt you. If I had been Mr. Jones today, instead of being polite and moderate, I would have insisted in not having Mr. Filipovic start giving evidence. I would have insisted. And I would have said, When I have finished reading those documents, then we can start hearing Mr. Filipovic's evidence. And I will suspend the sitting later on, after this first witness comes over, and we will decide what measure to adopt. Because this is -- I cannot accept this. You cannot expect to come here and present us with a situation whereby Defence counsel, who have already a hard case to deal with, all of a sudden have to go through a bundle of documents, not knowing whether they are going to be used or not, when the practice has always been that you inform the Defence well beforehand what documents you are going to use, documents which would have already been disclosed a long time ago, with which, supposedly, they are already familiar. I mean, I can't accept a situation like this. You would have found me much more difficult than Mr. Jones, I can assure you. And I appreciate Mr. Jones being moderate in his claims and not radical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again, with all respect to the argumentation of the Defence, I'm reacting upon the fact that argumentation is that it had not been disclosed prior, and my response to it, that this material has been disclosed. And when it comes to an exhibit list, we try to update the Defence counsel as soon as possible of the exhibits we would like -- prefer to use, and according to the court guideline, that's a day in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should have brought another witness, or other witnesses instead, this one and the one we have tomorrow. But you can't expect to draw blood from the Defence. I mean, I won't allow it. We will end up with having the witness of Mr. Filipovic and having the testimony of the next one. They can sit pretty and say: We haven't had time to go through these documents. You start making use of some of those documents, maybe yes, maybe not. They will reserve their position. Both Mr. Filipovic and the other one will go back to where they have come from, and then within a month or so, we will have another motion asking for their recall. In the meantime, you would have fresh documents, and so on and so forth. This is not how cases are conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all respect, my first reply was referring to the disclosure, and the disclosure, I clarified the position to that extent, that we've already disclosed material from the 3rd of October. Now the exhibit list, those documents, that's another issue. And if you want to clarify that, I can give the floor to Ms. Sellers, who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I first, Your Honour, just note two things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, the chronology which we prepared in relation to the Ms. Trifunovic document is informative in this regard: in that it indicates when we received materials to inspect and when they were disclosed. Mr. Wubben is referring to a date in October 2004 and he's referring to disclosure of rules of the road files, which, as you know, start with RR. I just look at the first few documents here. None of them are RR there. They're simply not rules of the road documents. So to claim that these have all been disclosed as rules of the road documents, I think Mr. Wubben and his team, first of all, before simply wildly asserting that this has all been disclosed, to check ERN number by ERN number, receipt by receipt, and check whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, if this goes on I will suspend the case until the house is in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it's simply to say this: that it's not helpful for the Prosecution simply to assert that it's all been disclosed to us. Let them check first and then they'll see what the real position is. Otherwise it's simply not helpful to have the discussion we're having today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is an unnecessary, unnecessary incident, and unnecessary concerns for the Trial Chamber, for the Defence. It's simply -- yes, Ms. Sellers. I thought Mr. Wubben was passing on --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Let me first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Let me first react. I did not simply state that it has all been disclosed. What I stated is that I regret that I'm not able to check it to the full extent, but at least I've now been informed that a chunk, or most of it, has been disclosed from the 3rd of October. And then again I offered additional information regarding the exhibits from Ms. Patricia Sellers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree in terms of the confusion. My information from the case manager, it all has been disclosed on October 3rd under rules of the road. The reason there are no RRs on those is that they were included with -- in some of the materials that rules of the road have that don't have RR. I think this is slightly beside the issue that Defence counsel has brought up and one that we want to address. If the issue are documents that might be used within the Prosecution's leading of the next witness, that could be possibly exhibits, well, my understanding is they have received our exhibit list that we will use with the next witness. You have received the specific exhibits that are used. So that's a slightly different issue, and my only point was not to conflate those two things, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but if they are not the same thing, they are not the same documents that are to be used, that's going beyond the exhibit list that you have tendered. In other words, if -- are these documents, according to you or according to your case manager, included in the list of exhibits that you have handed over, provided the Defence with, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibits that are on the exhibit list, the Defence has been provided with the ERN numbers. If any of those ERN numbers are contained in that bundle of documents, it would mean that the Defence has had those documents since October 30th. Those are two different things. If you mean whether we have provided them with the exact documents that will be used as exhibits, I believe the court practice is they are handed those documents in the Trial Chamber, but we've notified them as they notify us with the exhibit lists that they will use for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But basically, what we are faced with, Ms. Sellers, is -- let's come to the basic language here. Basically, it means, and I have been a Defence lawyer and I know exactly what this involves, basically it means that they have got to go through all those documents one by one, check whether they tally with the exhibit list that you have, check whether they have them in their records. If they are new documents, they have to read them or at least know what the substance of the contents is in case they are made use of in the course of -- and all this is happening in less than 24 hours before this witness is supposed to come and give evidence. Even the idea of giving the Defence that box full of papers, with the task of going through them, and then checking whether they are included or excluded from the list of exhibits that you have provided the Defence with, whether they are extra documents, not included, and there is, it's laborious. How can you expect them to come here a few hours after they have been provided with the box full of documents and pretend to remain silent and say, Okay, we will go ahead, as if nothing has happened, and we will not reserve our position. Of course they will reserve their position. What irks me is that if, later on, going through these documents, they feel the need to recall Mr. Filipovic or Mr. X tomorrow, and these two persons would have in the meantime gone back to where they came -- would have come from, it's an inconvenience for them to come over again. It's an inconvenience for all of us, because it's going to take another one or two days from our schedule, it's extra expense for the Tribunal, and it's no extra pay for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I take your points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's why I'm telling you, thank God Mr. Jones hasn't got a Mediterranean temper. Thank you. Are you ready with the next witness? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. If there's nothing further on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't -- I think I would close the chapter here. And of course, I don't even think I need to discuss. We will reserve your position. We will discuss later on amongst ourselves. And if there is any further step that needs to be taken, obviously it will need to be taken. But we need to discuss amongst ourselves a little bit on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope this will not be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it's any assistance at some stage, we have the cover letter which went with that box. That's the only other additional information. But I'm certainly ready for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not the next witness. It's the witness we had yesterday. So we don't need to go into private session while he walks in; no? Okay. So could you please bring the witness in. Thank you. Please don't be aggressive with him, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's certainly not my intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I remind the technicians that we have facial distortion. Okay. Thank you. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Rankic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be proceeding with your testimony. I hope you have had time to rest and that you are ready. We have got about another hour to go and then you can go back home. May I remind you that you are testifying on the basis, or pursuant to the same oath or solemn declaration that you entered yesterday, to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jones will be proceeding with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, in order to make progress today and to conclude your testimony as quickly as possible, I'd be grateful if, wherever possible, you would reply simply "yes," "no," or "I don't know," to my questions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if there's a pause at some stage, it may be because we're waiting for interpretation, so don't feel the need to add anything simply because we're waiting. It's simply a question of waiting for the interpretation. Now, I have a couple of preliminary questions before moving on to some other areas from yesterday's testimony. The first is: To your knowledge, do you have any Muslim enemies from your area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So as far as you know, none of them would have a motive to falsely accuse you of being involved in ethnic cleansing of Muslims in Voljevica and Zaluzje in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankic, in answer to my very first question about Bjelovac yesterday, you responded, and I'm quoting: "Bjelovac only had a handful of families, the ones that I mentioned. I think you're confusing this with Zaluzje, which is adjacent to Bjelovac. That seems to have been an error all long."

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question to you today is: Have you been discussing this case with other people who have testified before this Tribunal? In particular, have you discussed this case with Slavka Matic, from your village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps you can answer this: How can you refer to something being an error all along when it was the very first question that I put to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the 10 per cent you asked me about. My calculation was 10 per cent. I was actually trying to count the families. That's what I had in mind. I'm not sure if we understood each other properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You spoke to Slavka Matic, did you not, and she told you that there was a question of how many Muslims lived in Bjelovac, and that's why you were referring to something being an error all along, referring to her testimony as well as yours.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Never mind. I'll move on. Yesterday you told us that the Territorial Defence was so disorganised in 1992 that people could just desert if they wanted to, whereas that changed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the usher could please show the witness Defence Exhibit D92 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll direct your attention to the fourth page in the original, also page 4 in the English. The ERN is 0132-0786. And we see at 135 Bibic, Miloje deserted in January. Now, my question is: Doesn't this show that the Serb military authorities took great care to keep track of persons who did desert, even in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did happen also in 1992, but in 1993, you would have been taken to account. You could have been gaoled or something. Back in 1992, from May onwards, you could have just gone away without anyone touching you and coming back whenever you liked. So that was the reason I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: While we're with this document, I'd refer you to page 0132-0790. You need to turn four pages. We have the fourth ceta, and again your name at the top, Slavoljub Nedja Rankic, as commander. And then in the third vod, number 271, we see Zoran Rajic. Now, do you know Zoran Rajic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last name doesn't ring a bell. Zoran certainly does, but not the last name. Rajic? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It says Dobrovoljac. So he was a volunteer from Serbia, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So he certainly wasn't guarding his village, was he? Because his village was in another country, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to us as a refugee. He was staying with some relatives, and then that village fell, and he came over. Or at least, that's the story he gave us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A refugee from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had been staying with relatives in Bosnia and then the war started, and he then got involved with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this is -- you know Zoran, then? He's the volunteer on that document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know Zoran, but I can't remember his last name. It was, after all, a long time ago, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can leave that document to one side. Now, you told us yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones. Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just would have a question. Can you identify the date of this document? It's difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's December 1992, Your Honour. It appears on the first page of the English version and the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Since this document refers to the 22nd of December, 1992, it appears as if this document has been established later, at least not during December, perhaps at the end of December, or could --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It could certainly be the end of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Or even in January?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I believe any reference to January is January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. May I provide an explanation for this? There is a lot of information on these documents. Back in our country, the usual thing to do is for salaries to be paid retroactively. Salaries are paid in January for December, at the beginning of January, the salaries for December. If that's any help. Therefore, this document was probably produced in late December, must have been produced in late December.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankic, you told us yesterday that the road between Bjelovac and Bratunac in December 1992 was in Muslim hands. You said of that road, and I'll quote: "In May it was safe. No provocations. You could go from Bjelovac to Bratunac and back. But in June, the provocations started, ambushes and so on, so it was no longer safe." Now, my question for you is this: People who control a road don't have to ambush it, do they? They can set up roadblocks. Isn't it true that the Serbs held the road, but that it was occasionally ambushed by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used that road, the Bjelovac-Bratunac road. We were free to move about for a while. And then later on, at some point in June, one of our vehicles took the men and women over to Bratunac to buy some goods, and there at the so-called Zaluzje, an ambush took place, and the citizens who were inside that vehicle were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My point is this: The Muslims weren't passing freely back and forth between Bjelovac and Bratunac, were they? At the most, they were ambushing the road. They certainly didn't control the road, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. No one was allowed to go, but I have no idea who was in control. It wouldn't have been safe for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you referred to the school in Bjelovac yesterday, which you said was used to feed refugees from Loznica and Sikiric. Now, firstly, as you accepted yesterday, and I refer to page 80, lines 14 to 16, for Ms. Sellers's benefit, where I asked: "Sikiric, the Muslims were expelled from Sikiric in May 1992, were they not?" And you answered yes. It was Muslims who were expelled from Sikiric, not Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims at the Bjelovac school, no. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... expelled from Sikiric, not Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Donji Sikiric, yes, but not from Gornji Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's no such thing as Donji Sikiric and Gornji Sikiric, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donji Sikiric is on the road, on the main road, and Gornji is up above the road. That is usually referred to as Gornji Sikiric, or at least that's the term that we use.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you've said that the school was used just as a soup kitchen, essentially, for refugees, the school in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So if a cook working in the school at the time were never to mention refugees but were to say that she prepared meals for paramilitary units in the school, would that be untrue?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wouldn't be bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you repeat your answer, please. I'm not sure if the interpretation was correct.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were staying there, refugees from Sikiric and Loznica. They were staying there and eating there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were paramilitary units also staying there, and soldiers, and being fed there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who came from Bratunac, yes, from time to time. Not all the time; from time to time. They spent a couple of days there and then leave again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So yesterday, when you were speaking of the school and you said it was for refugees, you were telling at most a partial truth, weren't you? You weren't telling us the whole truth about what that school was used for?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did say that. Maybe you got me confused at the time. Maybe I didn't make myself clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just remind you that you're here to tell the whole truth, not just the bit that suits you. So if you'll please answer the whole truth when you answer questions. It's right, isn't it, in fact, in December 1992 and before, the school was the command centre for the military units in Bjelovac? And again you can answer yes, or no, or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I put it to you, and you can again simply reply yes or no, or you don't know, is that in December 1992, you on the Serb side in Bjelovac had a depot or depots of weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ammunition, a depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You had two battalions of soldiers, a 2nd and a 4th Battalion -- Battalions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying about these battalions. We only had a company, and it was called Independent Company. But there was no sort of battalion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Company. So what, about approximately 160 soldiers or more?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, thereabouts, ranging from 100 to 140 soldiers. Soldiers, fighters. Fighters is what we call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And also on the road which your unit secured, there were APCs, tanks, and transporters passing between -- well, let me rephrase that. That there were -- there was a presence of APCs, tanks, and transporters in the Bjelovac area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The APCs were there to protect the convoy en route to Bratunac, transporting food to Bratunac and back. That's what the APCs were there for, to provide security along the Bratunac-Bjelovac road.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What about tanks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One tank and two APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And there was also heavy artillery in Sikiric, among other places, which was firing on Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the water treatment plant in Kunjerac. In your statement to the Prosecutor, to the investigators in 2000, you said: "There was no special protection for the water treatment plant." Now, I'm going to ask you a question about that in a moment. If we could first just see where Kunjerac is. We can use the map we used yesterday, with the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please, the map. Mr. Jones, could you indicate to the usher where it is yourself so that he will focus the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The water treatment plant was near the school, and there was a pool at Kunarac, if that's what you're asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm asking about Kunjerac. Could you point to Kunjerac on the map, please, with a pointer, on the electronic monitor. Do you see Biljaca? Do you see Bjelovac? Yes, there we go.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's very near Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the hill, just above Bjelovac. Just there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just a few hundred metres from Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that Kunjerac was in fact a stronghold, and that there was an anti-aircraft top, i.e., heavy artillery, on Kunjerac, on the hill?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. There were a couple of those, whatever we call them, trenches, that we used as protection for Kunjerac to keep people from coming there. Even after the pipe had burst, the trench remained to protect the pool or reservoir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wasn't there a unit of Red Berets, an elite unit from Serbia, based in Kunjerac at this time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if the usher would assist by showing the witness Exhibit D86. This is the document which we saw with another witness. The ERN, for the record, is 0132-0961. It dates from November 1992. And in the middle, one sees the words in the original "Prva ceta crvene beretke Kunjerac," in English, "Kunjarac Red Berets, 1st Company."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that it was there the Red Berets, the intervention unit from Bratunac, they would come to our area every now and then. I don't know about any other such unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But weren't they in fact fighting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who were the Red Berets? Were they locals from Bratunac or not, the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were people from Bratunac. They were some sort of a reconnaissance platoon that was used to carry out reconnaissance and for assistance. We call them the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll be able to throw some light on that with the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. Sorry for having interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. The next exhibit, the ERN is 0132-1081. In fact, we're going to combine two exhibits in one. The other one has the ERN 0132-1103. If those could be shown to the witness. If the witness would look at, when he has it, the document, one sees the name Miodrag Cvijic, born in 1972, from Novi Sad or Zablje, from Serbia, in any event, died 14 December 1992 in Voljevica, in combat. Red Beret. And then at the bottom it says that he died during enemy attack while performing a combat assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before I ask you a question about that, I'll also pass on to the next exhibit. Radoslav Djukic, from Pakrac, which you might be able to help us with that, Mr. Rankic, but I believe it's in the Krajina, seriously wounded and later died in a counter-attack in Voljevica on 14 December 1992, and he's a Red Beret as well. Now, seeing those documents and those dates, does that help you with the question of whether they were fighting in the Bjelovac area on the 14th [Realtime transcript read in error"4th"] of December, 1992? Perhaps you know these individuals even.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these persons, nor do I know anything at all about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two separate numbers, Mr. Jones, or one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think they -- yes, two separate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the first one will be the one which was tendered first, and that is the document relating to Miodrag Cvijic. This document is being tendered and admitted and marked as Defence Exhibit D94.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one correction for the record. I believed I said 14th of December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- earlier. That's perhaps how it should read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not the 4th of December

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 14th, I heard you say 14th of December. The second document being tendered, admitted and marked as Defence Exhibit D95 is the document which relates to the record sheet of Radoslav Djukic, who died on the 14th of December, 1992. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're now going to show the first of two video segments, and by way of explanation, the video is from the Bratunac Brigade collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which church provided you with these?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Probably the Orthodox church, Your Honour, although I can't confirm. It's from the Bratunac Brigade collection. And the number is V000-3937, which the Prosecution has. And it's clear from the original that it concerns the action in Bjelovac on 14 December 1992. I'll just say, for the benefit of the Prosecution and for the record, on the original, at 01:25:18, there's a white board which says "Bratunac 14 December 1992." I'm going slowly for the interpreters. At 1:26:40 of the video, a journalist is reporting on the action in Bjelovac on the 14th of December, 1992, and he's in Bratunac as bodies are arriving there. And we haven't edited the video. We're showing segments, but it hasn't been edited by us. So if we could play the first segment. Yes, and if the technical booth could switch over to Defence mode. Yes, we can go ahead on "Computer Evidence."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We can stop there with that segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We heard from that clip that Slobodan Despotovic had died there. Do you know that a Slobodan Despotovic was killed in the Serb counter-attack in Voljevica on the 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with the name or with what happened. I only know about Bjelovac. I didn't leave Bjelovac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, if we could look at Exhibit D87, in order just to fix the time. We see three names down -- ERN 0066-1863, Slobodan Despotovic, CV, died in Voljevica on the 14th of December, 1992, "labodbi kontranapad," which is in combat, counter-attack. And then we also see Zlatan Bogicevic, also died on the 14th of December, 1992, in Voljevica, in the counter-attack. And then further down, Milorad Tosic, dying in Bjelovac on the 14th of December, 1992. It says "u borbi odbrana," so defence in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Are you aware that Red Berets were fighting in Bjelovac on the 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't there on that day. Had they been there, everything would have turned out differently, because they were capable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just for the record, I also direct Your Honours' attention to D45, line 102, which confirms the death of Slobodan Despotovic in Voljevica. There's no need to look at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, isn't it right, Mr. Rankic, that on the 14th of December, 1992, that there was a fierce counter-attack by Serb forces, including Red Berets, counter-attacking from Voljevica towards Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that day. I only knew about Bjelovac, because that's where I was. I have no idea what was happening in Voljevica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. Sorry. Let's turn to the action of the 14th of December, 1992. You told us yesterday that you were expecting an attack by Muslim forces. You just didn't expect them to attack from this side of the Drina. So my question is: They took you by surprise, didn't they? Otherwise you would have put up a better fight.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's perfectly clear. I have nothing to add. Of course, we didn't know there would be an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the first thing that happened on the 14th of December, 1992, as far as you're concerned, was that you heard shots. So you don't actually know how the action started, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in your statement in the year 2000 to the Tribunal investigators - I'm looking at page 2, ERN 00939359, four to five lines from the bottom - you said: "The shooting was so intense that I could not tell if any of the villagers were returning fire." So you don't know, do you, whether there was actually a fierce, two-way fight?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To your knowledge, you don't know --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is to confirm that there was heavy shooting, but I couldn't see everything from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned yesterday that you saw a group of ten or so people in uniform outside Nikola Petrovic's house.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, first of all, you have no idea who those people are or were, do you? You weren't able to identify any attackers? Again, a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they were Muslims. There was nothing else that I could assume. I never saw anybody personally, nor did I know anybody personally, and I said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And when you saw these people, Nikola Petrovic's house was already on fire and these people were outside the house, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday, and it's the truth, that I saw it from the yard. When I saw the smoke coming from the yard, in the direction of Nikola's house, I went up to the upper storey to see where the smoke was coming from, and I saw Nikola's house, and I saw that it was certainly 100 per cent Nikola's house. So that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My point is this: You didn't see anyone set fire to that house, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't. I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For all you know, the fire could have started from a grenade or mortar fire or some other non-human cause, for all you know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't check it out. I just noticed the people I saw what I saw. I didn't say that they had set fire to it. I just assumed they did. Who else could it have been? They were the people there. Now, who these people were, well...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm simply trying to establish where you made assumptions and what you actually know. Now, going back to those people outside Petrovic's house, whom you described yesterday as capering and pulling faces, you didn't see them communicating with other groups of soldiers, did you? And again, a yes or no answer is sufficient, or I don't know. Did you see that group of people communicating with other groups?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw other people -- actually, I just saw the people I saw. I didn't see any other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So you didn't see them communicating with others, coordinating their actions with others, or anything of that nature, did you? You saw them capering outside someone's house.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard some voices. I did hear that. And I couldn't make out what they were saying. I heard some names, too. But voices, saying something. But I didn't dare stand around watching too much, because I was afraid for my own safety. That's why I was a bit wary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When it was suggested yesterday to you by His Honour that you saw a coordinated attack of soldiers coordinating their actions, that's not something you saw at all, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this in legal terms. I'm an ordinary citizen, an ordinary person, and I can't enter into this discussion with you. I just told you in my own words. I can't tell otherwise than using my own words. I can't explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, on that day, the Serbs gathered in the centre of Bjelovac, you told us, and that's because the people who attacked Bjelovac were not able to reach the centre on that day, were they? The attackers didn't reach the centre of Bjelovac on the 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attackers? You mean -- I can't understand this. I'm not following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. The attackers did not reach the centre of Bjelovac, where you gathered that evening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening, you mean? They went -- the house we had gathered at was up by the road, and they held the communication, the road towards the Drina. So they went down by the Drina and round that way, except for Nikola's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: They had to withdraw from Bjelovac, didn't they, on the 14th of December, because of a fierce counter-attack by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there were no further attacks. At around 1800 hours, everything stopped. You couldn't hear anything anywhere. It was quiet. So I assume that those attackers had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have little time. So we'll play the next segment of a video, the same video. It's a continuation of what we just saw. And it's a couple of minutes long, two or three minutes. If you could watch the video, please, Mr. Rankic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could counsel just clarify as to whether the wording or the transcription of the video, if he intends that to be part of what's offered into evidence or are we merely asking him to look at the visuals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, a very pertinent question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I've understood it entirely. We would be tendering these clips, which have subtitles. I was going to read the subtitles into evidence. Will you give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it that this will receive an exhibit number, a Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to raise a Defence objection as to the substance. I can understand the translation, the wording, but as to the truth of to what that wording is, there certainly hasn't been any evidence of that. And then just the last issue I'd like to raise, a bit more in general. I think it was counsel who testified as to the location of the tapes and of the scenes that we're seeing. I don't see where the witness has recognised a place that these scenes are taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if he recognised this road, believe me, I wouldn't believe him, because you can barely see anything. I mean, it could be a naive painting, as it shows on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It will emerge from what follows where the film is shot. And in the last sequence we had the -- where someone died and that was placed as being in Voljevica. So we have clues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a town, I mean, or a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I certainly don't wish to give evidence, it was simply to try and assist where the clips came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with these at the end. Let's proceed first and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're going to pause at certain places. Pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday, Mr. Rankic, about Svetozar Andric, who was commander of the Bircanska Brigade and at the time of the commanded a special assault unit. Do you recognise that man to be Svetozar Andric on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this man at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We see some of the soldiers wearing the kokarda in the picture.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These are Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say so. I can't check it out. How do you want me to do that? Perhaps they are; perhaps they're not. What can I say? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which other ethnic group wore kokarde? Which other ethnic group, soldiers, wore kokarde, apart from the Serbian? Did the Muslims wear a kokarde?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Croats? Did the Croats wear a Kokarda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the Serbs did wear a Kokarda, or some units of the Serbian armed forces wore a Kokarda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's right. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we see soldiers wearing a Kokarda in this clip, you would suppose that they are Serbian soldiers and not soldiers belonging to other ethnic groups; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say that the soldiers of the paramilitary formations were wearing that, not any regular soldiers, as far as I can remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Serbian paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll continue with the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, stop there. For the record, I'd like to just read the subtitles into the record. Of course, excepting what the Prosecution is saying, that it doesn't constitute evidence and the truth of what's being said. We have: "Gunner, can you hear me? Do not take your head out and listen to me. Where this house is burning and from that house go 50 metres forward and watch out. You know those houses you were blowing out yesterday? Do not take your head out and listen to me. Where this house is burning, and from that house, go 50 metres forward and watch out. You know those houses you were blowing out yesterday. So you go 50 metres more. Means until this pole here. And up there from the right, straight away, in the houses." I think in fact that should read "straight towards the houses," but we can check that. "Do not target down. Do not shoot yet. You target houses up there. If you throw over, you will hit Bjelovac, and especially up there, these houses to the right, below this peak we were shooting at yesterday. Do you remember? And tell the driver to go another 50 metres forward. Gunner, tell me if you can see it now. Not this house. There is a sniper man from the right. Do you know where he was yesterday?"

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, my question is, Mr. Rankic, first of all, do you recognise this area as being in the Bjelovac area, from what we've seen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recognise it on the basis of a picture like this. Maybe it was, but I really don't know. I don't know when this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware that Serb gunners were targeting houses in the Bjelovac area in the counter-attack on the 15th of December, 1992, and hitting houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Also, referring there to a sniper in a house who they're trying to dislodge, are you aware that the Serb army would shoot buildings where they suspected snipers were, in order to knock them out?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that at all. All I know is what happened from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll just play one more segment. It's just a minute and a half or so, a couple of minutes maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, can you look at that face, the face of that young man. I asked you yesterday about Novo Ilic. Do you recognise that as Novo Ilic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be him, yes. It looks like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that transporter we see behind, is that the sort of transporter you were referring to as seeing on the road between Bjelovac and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Play again the final segment. It's just another minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we see somebody who appears to be Borivoje Tesic there. Do you recognise Borivoje Tesic on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You do know, don't you, that he was the newly appointed commander of the Bratunac Brigade when it was created on the 14th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the record, I think I should just read the subtitles into the record: "There was a grouping of forces that are retreating towards Srebrenica. We are helping our forces in the area of Bjelovac and Kunjerac. In less than an hour we are going to reach our aim and to connect with the forces in the area of Bjelovac and Kunjerac." My question is: Aren't these people that we're seeing well armed, well equipped, organised Serb soldiers from Bjelovac participating in a counter-attack on Bjelovac on the 15th of December, 1992? If you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please, I understand counsel's intention, but just in terms of phrasing, I don't think there's been anywhere on this video, even if we do assume that the words that are spoken are true, that indicates that they come from Bjelovac. That's just certainly not been anything said in this video. So I would just ask you to rephrase the question that you have just put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we did see Novo Ilic, who we saw in an earlier document, who was in the Bjelovac TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If you do mean a someone, a person who originates from a town, that's different. Are you talking about that those troops are coming from the town? Then please clarify that for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Sellers is perfectly right. I would suggest you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed. I can omit to mention they're from Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What we're seeing here are well armed, well equipped, organised Serb soldiers participating in a counter-attack towards Bjelovac on the 15th of December 1992? If you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's go back to Novo Ilic for a moment. We have photographs, still photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could the usher assist, please, by distributing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can start asking the question, Mr. Rankic. You told us yesterday that Novo Ilic -- we saw that he was in the same Bjelovac TO as you. We saw that in D90, Exhibit D90, ERN 0132-0428. The question is: Did you have a nice uniform like Mr. Ilic did in this picture, on the day?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. On what day are you referring to, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On the 14th of December, 1992; 14th, 15th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a uniform, not like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could this picture be given a Defence exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be Defence Exhibit D96.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just a few more questions. Yes, I believe I was going to tender these segments of the video. I don't know if that's actually been done. If not, I would tender the segments which we've shown as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I just ask you: Did you refer to D90?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: D90. It bears a date of July 1992, whereas the video has to do with December 1992. What is the connection between these two dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question -- sorry. I'll wait for the interpretation. This witness and Novo Ilic were in the same TO Bjelovac, albeit in July 1992. We see Mr. Ilic is wearing a uniform there. My question was: Given that at some point, in any event, they were in the same unit, did Mr. Rankic also have a proper uniform such as Mr. Ilic had. And the witness replied that he didn't have a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the suggestion, I take it, is if Mr. Ilic was there, Mr. Rankic ought to have been there too. But Mr. Rankic has not confirmed that. Now, the -- yes, Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the witness answered when you were asked if you had such a nice uniform: "No, I did not have such a uniform." Did you have any kind of uniform at all, or were you only wearing your civil clothes when you were guarding or commanding the part of the guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have a uniform of the former Yugoslav army, and it was the olive-green-type uniform. That's the kind I had; trousers and shirt and cap. It was called the Tito cap, Titovka. I was a reservist then and that's the uniform I had, and that's the uniform I wore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the sequence of clips that we have seen are being tendered and received in evidence as Defence Exhibit D97, 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And thank you for that question clarifying the issue of the uniforms. Perhaps just one further clarification which follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These uniforms, the uniform being worn by Novo Ilic and the one being born by Mr. Tesic are not the olive-grey uniforms of the JNA, are they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we can remove the video now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that video, we heard Serb soldiers talking about shooting at houses, blowing up houses. I put it to you - if you can help us with this, then please do - but the fact is the Serb counter-attack caused the majority, if not the totality, of the destruction of houses that you saw after the 14th of December, 1992, in Bjelovac and Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't check that out, because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just a few final questions. You told us a lot yesterday about how you learned from other villagers how Muslim forces, on the 14th of December, 1992, had split in two, and there was a third group who went elsewhere, and you even drew it on the map for us. It's right, isn't it, that none of that is based on your personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the locals told us from Loznicka Rijeka that fled and came to us. I didn't say that. They told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So if their information is wrong, you simply wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also told us that when the attack on the 14th started, that you basically tried to save your skin; you fled for your life. But in relation to that, I want to ask you if you recall making a statement to Judge Vaso Eric, Investigating Judge of the Lower Court in Zvornik on the 22nd of December, 1994. Firstly, do you remember making a statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a little bit. It was a long time ago. Yes, I did give a statement. I vaguely remember, but not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll put to you what you may have said on that occasion, and you can say whether you agree or not. I quote, and for the English, it's the -- it's page 2, seventh paragraph: "I tried to organise the defence of the village right away. Among other things, I called my neighbour, Stoja Petrovic, and told her to go up to the attic of Nedeljko Damjanovic's house which had a good view of the entire village."

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't safe. It was the house next door to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that much is true. "I told her that once she was there, she should keep me informed about what was going on so that it would be easier for me to organise and run the village's defence, as we were surrounded on all sides." Now, is that correct, that account, more or less?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 100 per cent, but near enough. Do you want me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask you a question before you go on. Isn't that right that you must have had walkie-talkies or Motorolas or something to communicate with someone who is up in an attic while you're running around the town organising defences? She is not going to be shouting to you from the attic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have one. I didn't have a Motorola. I claim that for sure. I didn't have one. And they were houses, next-door houses. It would have been better had I had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. I would imagine there is a re-examination, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we can finish with the witness now. Do you have any questions? I don't have any questions either. Mr. Rankic, your testimony ends here, which basically means that you're free to go. You will be escorted by our usher to the room where you were waiting yesterday and today. But your testimony now is finished. On behalf of the Tribunal, I can assure you that you will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home. And on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and myself, and on behalf of the Tribunal in general, I should like to thank you for having accepted to come over and give testimony in this case. And may I also wish you on behalf of everyone here a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break. We'll reconvene 25 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I announced that Ms. Joanne Richardson will take my place, but I take the opportunity to clarify, because during the break, I tried to put everything in place, to the most extent. I had not so much time, but at least I come to the following: We disclosed on the 30th of November this box with documents. By the way, the box was presented as such to carry it more easily than just handing over like that, and it was well sorted, with an annex, and accessible as that. Now, this disclosure was meant to be a courtesy disclosure with a view to a chunk, a big, big file of rules of the road disclosure that had been done earlier, and this particular bunch of documents had been disclosed as taking out of this big file, with a view to the witness Filipovic. Now, I noticed by myself that there is a confusing reference by using the words that they may use as exhibits, and counsel is right for that. When you -- obviously as the Defence counsel point of view see it, you think by yourself, okay, it is the 30th of November. But by the way, we have to go through it. Your Honour, I apologise for not being so clear in that covering letter to the Defence. The following day, on the 1st of December, I recall myself that Madam Vidovic approached me and showed me a list of exhibits in the Filipovic witness overview. Well, Your Honour, she asked me: Is this an additional list, in addition to the exhibits, or does this replace the previous list? And I checked with my case manager. I promised her I will check this out and update you in the following break. I checked it out, and explicitly I told her that this is not in addition, this list, and it was a limited list, as I recall, I think I have a copy now, this is replacing, and she nodded yes, that she understood. And that list has also been sent through e-mail. After that, 1st of December, that was yesterday, and after that came second list, and the final version of it. Why I'm clarifying this, that at least yesterday there was a question raised by the Defence counsel, is this list of exhibits, is this in addition or is this replacing a first list? And now I understand more about the background of the question, but it had been put on notice as something to be questioned. And perhaps Madam Vidovic can further clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but this new list, does it contain those documents that are in that box?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are back to square one. They still have to go through that box, because the indication that they have been given is that they may be used during the testimony of Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Then I'm not clear enough. I'm sorry, Your Honour. It is -- my confirmation was that it is replacing, meaning for her, at least, that she could understand, so only these exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The exhibits on the list. And there was a limited number, referring to ERN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the purpose of the documents that are in that -- they were in that box? I don't see it any more. What's the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The purpose of the disclosure of that, of these documents, was of courtesy to give the Defence the documents that are part of a huge -- and we are disclosing hundreds of thousands of documents in the past to the Defence counsel team, as a kind of re-disclosure to them and to limit the relevant, from our searches point of view, the relevant documents to that extent. So to be limited to that purpose, and on the next day, at least any confusion should be clarified by my response to her question and her relevant question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to make use of any of those documents during the examination-in-chief of Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's -- I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No, in fact, I will not be making use of any of the documents that were re-disclosed to the Defence with respect to Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically the Defence need not even go through those documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, they can go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for the purpose of this witness, according to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, according to me, I will not be using those documents in the Prosecution's case in chief. Now, the Defence may want to use them. I don't know. But these were documents that were provided to them previously, and we just thought as a courtesy to the Defence that they would want to have a specific stack of documents related to that witness. Certainly, if the Defence had gone through the disclosure that we previously made to them earlier in the year --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry. From the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. These documents will not be -- these documents will in fact be familiar to them. These documents are not ones that they would have been seeing for the first time as of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, we believe that Mr. Wubben should pay closer attention to what's going on within the OTP. So far, I have written at least 30 letters in relation to untimely disclosure or failure to disclose pursuant to the Rules. I will not elaborate on this now. I have always requested that we be treated fairly, especially in relation to our own actions. Believe me, Your Honours, I found these documents in my locker last night, at 2.00. It is true that this receipt carries the date of the 13th, but I only found them yesterday, and we do go through our lockers at least three or four times a day. That's one thing. Secondly, this is an entirely different problem. On the 20th of July this year, we carried out an inspection and we managed to locate a whole series of documents in relation to a number of different witnesses, not only in relation to Mr. Filipovic but to other witnesses as well. We kindly requested that these be forwarded to us on a number of occasions. Instead of being told yesterday that this is a group of documents in relation to that request we made, we received them together with a letter saying that these may be used. Therefore, I had no indication at all from the OTP that they were talking about these documents that we were after. Be that as it may, we shall go through these documents again, or at least that's what I assume, but I'm worried that there may be earlier statements that are -- that remain undisclosed, and that the same thing may happen again as happened with Witness Svetlana Trifunovic. Therefore, my only request to the OTP is to make an extra effort to locate these documents. I have had several conversations with Mr. Wubben about this, and we spoke recently. I asked him to go through the OTP's files. I kindly asked that if there were any further documents, sensitive documents, documents perhaps of an exculpatory nature in connection with Rule 68 and directly relating to witnesses, or statements pursuant to Rule 48, challenging the credibility of witnesses. Therefore, I will say this again: We do not want to aggravate our relations with the OTP, and I do not want to try the Trial Chamber with these issues. But can they just please go again through their files and enable us to have a fair trial. A fair trial means that we have access to all documents that might contain elements that are exculpatory for our client. So much for me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I -- are there any further remarks or can we close the incident now, hoping, hoping, that what we have been told at the end of the day is correct. Because I would hate to think for a moment that we end up with having a number of those documents actually being used by the Prosecution in the course of the examination-in-chief of Mr. Filipovic, because that would conflict matters at that point in time. Yes. Otherwise certainly the argument -- yes, Mr. Wubben. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, a point well taken, and I apologised already for the redaction. But again, I hope it is clarified in the order, and the clarification yesterday put forward to Madam Vidovic that there was a replacement, so there shouldn't be any confusion. But from the beginning, yes, indeed, the letter may raise questions and that's why perhaps she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can close the incident here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else about this witness before we bring him in?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There's nothing in particular with respect to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please bring in -- escort Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed any further, I want a confirmation from you that you are receiving interpretations of what -- interpretation of what I am saying in a language which you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence very soon.
