Before you do so, our Rules require that you make -- that you enter a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, in the sense that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is going to be handed to you now by the usher. Please read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please be seated. Let me explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. First of all, this is the trial against Naser Oric. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from Malta. To my right, I have Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt from Denmark; to my left, Judge Albin Eser from Germany. You will first be asked a series of questions by a member of the team for the Prosecutor, for the Prosecution. I suppose it's Ms. Richardson - correct me if I'm wrong - who probably has briefed you in these last few days and who, therefore. You know. She will then be followed by Madam Vidovic, who is lead counsel in defence of the accused Naser Oric. Your duty as a witness, even though you have been summoned as a witness by the Prosecution, is not to draw any distinction between the Prosecution and Defence, and to answer all the questions that are put to you by whoever, irrespective of whether the questions are put by the Prosecution or by the Defence, fully and truthfully. Because that is what you undertook to do when you made the solemn declaration. Having said so, I now ask -- call upon Ms. Richardson to start her direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Filipovic. I will proceed to ask you to confirm a number of facts with respect yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can lead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please confirm that you were born on April 1st, 1964; that you're married; you are a Serb; and you have two children; you formerly worked in a mine, the Sase mine, until April; and you are now unemployed. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you also lived in the village of Bjelovac, in the municipality of Bratunac, and you lived there until 14 December 1992, with your wife, parents, brother, and children; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just for the record, please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Slavoljub Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the village of Bjelovac, is this a Serb village, predominantly Serb village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's a mixed village. There were Muslim homes there as well as Serb homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many Serb homes there were in 1992 and how many Muslim homes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'd have to clarify something. Bjelovac is not a village; it's a compound, a conglomeration of a number of villages. It's a local commune. Myself, I come from the village of Loznica. Bjelovac is a local commune. In terms of percentage, it was predominantly Muslim. As for the village of Loznica, it was a predominantly Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In the village of Loznica, where you resided - and thank you for that correction - were there any Muslim homes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. About six homes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many homes in total were there in Loznica in 1992 and prior?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Loznica and Sikiric, about a hundred. Actually, 40 in Loznica, 40 homes. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And approximately how many people would you say resided in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Four or five persons per family, so I would say roughly about 200 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What did most of the residents of Loznica do for a living? Were they farmers or did they work in the mine, as yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them worked in the mine, and some were farmers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, what types of buildings would one find in Loznica? Was there a police station, a school, or any other type of government facility?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We had a health centre, a school, and a common home, as we called it, which was an institution in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you tell us, the surrounding villages of Loznica, or the hamlets, were they Muslim or were they Serbs or were they mixed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: With the exception of Sikirici, all were Muslim. Sikirici was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance, with Your Honour's permission, I'd like to ask that the witness be given this map, and I'm also requesting an exhibit number for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The sequential number is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit number will be P451.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this map is being tendered, received, and admitted in evidence, and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P451.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness just --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, if you can, just turn to the map and point out to the Trial Chamber where your village is located on that map. If possibly you could be given something, a pen. Thank you. And if you could just circle that, the village of Loznica.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Loznica?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you indicate for the Trial Chamber where your home was located, if you can find it, if you could approximate for us on the map where your home would have been located.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your village, did there come a time that there were tensions in your village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Tensions were felt as soon as the war broke out in Croatia, and after that, you could feel the stench of war and you could tell that war would come to us too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did there come a time that any of your neighbouring villages were attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what village are you referring to that was attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Cijepala and Loznica, the mountainous area over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could just ask the usher's indulgence to show the witness P451 again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you just indicate that village that you just referred to that was attacked on June 28th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. I only circled Loznica. Cijepala, it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it was in June of -- June 28th, 1992 that this village was attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you learn anything about who was responsible for the attack on that village, or did you learn anything about the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There was an attack organised by a commander. If you have no commander, you can't carry out an attack. I'm talking about command responsibility. It wasn't carried out just by random individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who did you learn was responsible? Who was the commander for that attack, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the village of Vlasenica, what happened to the residents of that village after the attack? Did they remain in the village or did they move elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Not Vlasenica. I'm talking about Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Eight people were killed - six men, two women - 16 wounded, and the rest retreated as far as this point right here, those who remained. And the rest fled to Serbia and never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did any of those people come to your village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was that because they had nowhere else to go? Did they have relatives there? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the relatives were up here in the mountain. When I moved here in 1960 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the year.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- there was not a single house there. So yes, most people had relatives in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did they seek housing in any other place in your village, for instance, a school, or any other facility?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Most of those whose relatives had been killed left for Bratunac, and so did the women.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, after June 28th, 1992, did there come a time that your village also faced violence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go direct, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that your village was also attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prior to the 14th of December, 1992, was your village attacked or was your village fired upon?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 14th of December, every day. It was under siege every day. Because from our village, there was not a single Serb house or Serb until Rogatica, until you got to Rogatica. They were all Muslims. There were 30.000 soldiers behind our backs. And we had no communication with Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell where the shooting was coming from? And if you could indicate for us on Prosecution Exhibit 451, the map that's next to you. Could you show us where the shooting was coming from on a daily basis. No need to write on the map. You can just point.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From Pirici, a machine-gun opened fire every day from Pirici, and from the forest as well, the edge of the forest. We were up by the road, and there was 150 metres from the Drina to one and a half kilometres, so it was the furthest point from the Drina to the forest, and they fired round the clock, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, before we get to the attack on the 14th of December, 1992, did there come a time that your village organised a village guard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just before the war broke out, or rather, the beginning of May, the beginning of May. And as the war escalated, the -- it started in Sarajevo, Zvornik, and moved towards us, the war did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who was part of this village guard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly people from the village, from Srebrenica too, who had come to visit their relatives, because Srebrenica remained pure. There were no Serbs there any more. So around Srebrenica, everything had been destroyed, the whole surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many men were in this village guard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was it 30, 40, 50, approximately, or even less than that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, people were in their own houses, round their own houses. What can I say? Not more than a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, were you -- did you have weapons, the village guards, and did you have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There were weapons. Uniforms? Well, depends. If anybody had uniforms, they were the ones that dated back to the TO. The commanders received camouflage uniforms in both armies, on both sides. But for soldiers, it was more difficult. It was difficult to come by uniforms. It was for the commanders' recreation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did everyone have a weapon, or did only some people manage to obtain a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. Not everybody had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you yourself have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where did you acquire this weapon, and what kind of weapon was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I bought it in 1990, 1991. At the beginning of 1991 I bought one, and it was only later, in 1993, that I was issued one from the army, at the end of 1993. Because, you know, Bjelovac, we were joined to Skelani, for example, Skelani and Bratunac. But nobody thought much about us. It was only when Bjelovac fell that we were joined to the Bratunac Brigade. Otherwise, no one gave us much thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did the village guard of your village receive any assistance from the Serb army? In other words, did you receive weapons, training, uniforms, prior to the attack on the 14th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because there's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I noticed something missing in the transcript which I am positive I heard the witness say, or at least the interpretation came that way. The previous question, he said, "Because, you know, Bjelovac, we were joined to Skelani, for example, Skelani and Bratunac. But nobody thought much about us. It was when Bjelovac..." and it stops there. However, I recall that he had said also, "It was when Bjelovac fell that we were joined to the Bratunac Brigade. Otherwise, no one gave us much thought." Is that what you said earlier on? It was when Bjelovac fell that you were joined -- that you were taken into the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because Bratunac is 7 kilometres away from us. And with this division, who made the division and who divided us up, I don't know, Skelani is 40 kilometres away from us. And it would have been normal to go to Bratunac and not Skelani to become part of Bratunac and not Skelani when Bjelovac fell and then the people went to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But I'm talking of the Bratunac Brigade. Were you joined with the Bratunac Brigade after Skelani fell -- after Bjelovac, after Bjelovac fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue. But it was important, because we will face it later on, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the village guard, did you organise in such a way that you had to patrol the village? And could you tell us how that was done. And explain to us what are the duties of a village guard.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly they were people standing guard round their own houses. You wouldn't go to sleep. You would be on duty. You would do shifts. Somebody would always stay awake.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So bringing you to December 14th, 1992, when your village was attacked, could you tell us what time that took place and what you were doing on that day.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, at 5.30, that was when the attack took place, and I was sleeping at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did you hear, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Shooting started coming from all sides. Everything was burning, on fire. Everything was -- they were shooting all over. They came from behind us, from our rear. They knew that the people would flee towards the Drina River, because it's 500 metres away from the road. And they were waiting for us to try and escape towards the Drina River. And then they just shot at us and killed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment. If you need to use the map, you can use the one that's right next to you, and you can point to where the shooting started when you first realised that the village was under attack. And possibly draw an arrow. You can just point to where it was coming from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. It seemed to be coming from all sides --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what were you doing --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- we were under siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You say it was about 5.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you with anyone? You were at home at the time. Were any of your family members present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was awake until 3.00 a.m., and then I went to bed. They took us by surprise. First of all, I thought they were owls, but I went to bed. And when the first shots were fired, I jumped up. My father was in the house with me, my brother was too, my mother, and two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did you do? At some point did you leave your home?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as I stepped outside the house, on the right-hand side, towards Sikiric, the next-door neighbour, people had stormed that house. My house is a new house and it looks towards the Drina. Just one floor, the ground floor level was -- construction was finished there. But they'd already gone to the Filipovic house. His wife managed to escape towards the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And let me stop you for a moment. When you say people had stormed that house, which house are you referring to, and could you tell us what people you're referring to. Could you describe them to us? Were they soldiers or civilians? Could you tell what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side. The house to the right of my house. Filipovic, my cousin, was killed, but his wife survived. His children weren't there, just him and his wife. And he was killed but his wife managed to escape. That's the next-door house to the right of my own house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who stormed the house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, because he didn't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The late Stevo's wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But you said before that they stormed the house. Could you tell us who is "they"? Were these the people who were attacking the village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I -- they were already in the house when I went outside. You could hear banging and things like that. They had already taken the house. Nobody had escaped. They were already in the house and had taken control of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And these were the people who were attacking; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you see them? Did you get a look at them from where you were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were in the house, inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then what happened? What else did you observe?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I observed that they had taken control of the area from the Drina, because on one side I saw them kill Milun Ilic from Srebrenica, for example. He was moving towards Slavko's house and he was killed on the way, and Bozo Todorovic too. They killed them all. There was shooting coming from the forest, from the woods, and these -- they were running towards the Drina. But the others were waiting for them like huntsmen and killed them as they came out, came that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So they were shot as they were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what else did you -- what else did you do after this, and what else did you observe?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I saw that they had taken control of the right-hand side, on the left, I was -- it was -- there was Bjelovac in the centre, towards the left. And when Milun was killed and Bozo Todorovic was killed, my father came to my house, Radovan Vucetic and Milenko. Radovan set out towards the Drina, towards an auxiliary facility that I had, and I said: Let's go. Or rather, he went. He didn't want to listen to me. And I just heard him scream and cry. He asked for help, but we weren't able to go up to him. I told my father and Milenko: There's no way out. What are we going to do? I'm going to look for help, going to the centre of the village. Now, whether Radovan crawled on his own and managed to reach a shed, he was found there, his legs had been blown, shot. But when I arrived, nobody dared go up there. I returned to the Damjanovic house, actually, to Slavko Rankic's house, crawling along. I had to crawl along under fire all the time. And there was a machine-gun positioned 300 metres from the house, and it was firing at the village. So I went into Slavko Rankic's house there. There were some women there, elderly people. One person was wounded. And so I went back to Nedeljko Damjanovic's house, where I came upon Dara, that is to say, the wife of a cousin of mine called Stevo who had already been killed. And I saw that my pigs were going along the road. They had opened all the outhouses. And in 10 or 15 minutes, the house went up in flames.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Which house went up in flames?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My house did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where was your father at this time, and the other family members? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My father stayed in the new house, my new house, the one I was building. And the other family member stayed inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you said the house went up in flames, could you -- do you know if the other family members were still in the house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything of what had happened to them at all after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know who set fire to the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness didn't say anyone set fire to the house. He said he saw it in flames. It shouldn't be suggested to him that someone set fire to his house when he hasn't given that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What did you observe of your home from Slavko Rankic's house? Did you see your house, and could you tell what had happened to it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could see my house. It was 150 metres away, not even 200 metres, so yes, I could see it. So in my house, they stayed in my house, and in a short space of time, the house started to burn, just like all the other ones next door, the next-door houses. Everything was up in flames when I left at 5.30 in the morning, when I went outside, the Jovanovic houses, Loznicka Rijeka, and Sikiric, those houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you left the home of Slavko Rankic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just to go to Nedeljko Damjanovic's house. It's next door, 5 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I just have one other question with respect to your house. You said that the house started to burn. Do you know what caused it to burn?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know who set fire to it? Did you see the person?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the person who set fire to it. The attackers, those who attacked, they set fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that you went to the home of Nedeljko Damjanovic. Could you tell us what happened when you got to his home, to his house.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. The attack went on the whole day. I stayed there until dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was anyone else there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There was Dara Filipovic and Stoja Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were they injured?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Dara was, yes. Stoja wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you see what was happening in the village while you were in Nedeljko Damjanovic's house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was shooting. All you could see was their heads. They took -- they were behind a shelter, but you would see a head come up, shooting. And that's what happened, and that's what happened the whole day. It went on the whole day. And most of the people were killed early in the morning in the first onslaught, by 8.00. Later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were able to see who the attackers were, whether they were soldiers or civilians, and how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon, I just saw one man wearing a camouflage uniform when he was coming out of Slavko Matic's house, Slavko Matic's house. He had a backpack on his back and a band of some kind. It was towards dusk, but he had a bandanna around his head; blue, I think. I couldn't see the rest. They were shooting from a vantage point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell approximately how many there were of the attackers, people who were shooting, at any point, from the time you left your home to when you were in either of the houses in the village? If you know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there must have been about a thousand of them, certainly, because there was shooting all over. It was real fireworks going on. Everything was ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And while you were in Nedeljko Damjanovic's house, were you able to see anything else, see individuals taking anything or anything with respect to the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could see that. Whether I saw somebody that I could name, I couldn't. I mean, I didn't see anybody's face up close, so I couldn't name any names, because it was a hundred metres away. You can't really recognise an individual at a distance of a hundred metres, particularly as they were shooting from a cover. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you see anyone carrying anything out of the village, taking anything away from the houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that day when they were withdrawing from Jovanovic's house, they were taking things away, and that's here [indicates]. What did they take? Well, you couldn't take any valuables, really, and goods weren't important. What was important was lives. But you could see they were taking things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And these people that were taking things, these were not people from your village. Were these part of the people who were attacking your village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the people who were attacking.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that the attack ended? And before you answer that, let me just ask another question. Did there come a time that you were shooting during this attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I shot when somebody would -- when I saw somebody's head rise up above the cover, I would shoot. But we had to keep them at a distance, keep them away, keep them away from us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what time did the attack end?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when it got dark, at night, dusk. That's what happened in all the villages. The attack went on during the day, and then they would withdraw as night fell, when it's night-time. Then there was a lull and it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you learned that this is what happened with other villages that had been attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it was like everywhere; Zaluzje, Loznica, and the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you left -- after the attack, you came out of Mr. Damjanovic's house, and what did you see?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really see anything. I couldn't get up to the house. I didn't have anyone to go with, so I went home. I went to the Petrovic house. And there were some women there, women in the village. They were getting ready to go to Serbia. I saw that there were none of my own people there, my own relatives. So Husic Novak, we took one of the wounded people off, but he died en route. He was there the whole day. We got to the boat. I don't know who was in the boat or how many of us were there or how we managed to take people across. But I went to Serbia. And the people were waiting for us along the road. There were lots of women and children, children going to school. The women were in Serbia with them. They went to Vrhpolje, to school there. They waited to see what was happening and who would turn up. It was hell-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you indicate for us on the map where you crossed the Drina, or the river, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you put your initials against that line that you just drew, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this is the Drina River that you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to have it -- yes. The witness has, for the record, put his initials, SF, on the line, which is visible on the map D451, to the left of Grabovica, across the River Drina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many people did you cross the river with after the attack, and did you cross over in a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- boat? I'll repeat the question. How many people did you cross the river with after the attack that day, and did you cross over in a boat?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In a boat, yes. Well, there were lots of people. Well, you can't get more than ten people in a boat. I crossed over. I don't know how long the evacuation went on for, how long they went on transporting the people across the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So there were a number of people on the Bosnian side of the river waiting to cross over?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there also come a time prior to your leaving the village after the attack that there were soldiers, Serb soldiers, that appeared, prior to your crossing over?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. At dusk some soldiers came. But that was when I left. I didn't ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know if they stayed, if those Serb soldiers stayed in your village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Bjelovac did not fall entirely on the 14th. The next day there was shooting, on the 15th. They stayed until the evening of the 15th, and it was then that everyone was evacuated or had fled by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Everyone meaning all of the residents from the village left?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Whoever was still there. I don't know who specifically. I didn't return the next day. When they started ferrying the bodies across the river, I was at the Drina. They were ferrying across boatfuls of dead bodies. But they didn't allow me to go, because they knew what had happened in my house and that I was left alone. They were bringing bodies, my brother, and my father, I'm not sure when they brought him. The first time I saw his body was at the morgue in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would like to play a video clip that was played yesterday by the Prosecution. I believe that was Prosecution Exhibit 432.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If we could have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, do you recognise what's in this video that was just played to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You can see my house on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And is that how it looked on the day -- on December 14th, 1992, when your village was attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you just mentioned, Mr. Filipovic, your father. Could you tell us when you first discovered that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I realised that he had been killed right away, 7.00 in the morning. No one came out of the house, so I knew they must have been killed. I was 100 per cent certain when I saw him at the chapel in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what day was that that you saw him, his body?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And from his injuries, could you tell that he had died violently?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: He had been hit in the chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Hit by what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Rifle, rifle bullet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you learn what happened to your brother?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: He had also been shot in the neck. It was an entry-and-exit wound, straight through the neck. Probably he had been wounded for some time, because his hands were full of grass and earth when they brought him across to Serbia. Probably he had been wounded during the night, but there was no one to help him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when did you first observe his body?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th, the morning of the 15th, when they started to ferry Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the bodies across.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, did you ever learn what happened to your wife and children, and could you tell us the ages of your children at that time, the day the village was attacked, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My son was six months old, and my daughter, three years old. I knew nothing of their fate. I thought they burned alive in the house. However, when I came to Serbia, there was a lady who said something about them jumping into the Drina River, that their mothers threw them into the river. And this was the only thing I learned. For about ten days, I was certain that this was indeed what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When did you learn that this was in fact not true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Seven or eight days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did you learn happened to them, that they were not -- they hadn't drowned in the Drina, but what were you told about their fate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: They told me that they had been captured and were now in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who captured them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Whose army, or which army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did you do after you learned that they were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I found out when Naser joined in a conversation with a police officer, on a bridge, via radio, and he said that they had been captured and that they were with him. I was in some sort of a trance. I was taking medication. I was drinking a lot of alcohol. I was receiving treatment. I was emaciated; I weighed only 40 kilos. When I saw footage of myself in those days, I couldn't believe my eyes, I couldn't believe it was me. And across the bridge there was a woman who worked in a shop. She knew me. I came there and she was the first to break the news, that lady, that they were alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And other than being alive, did you know where they were being held or where they were located?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica. I knew they were in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who did you believe was responsible for them being in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate question, really. Who did you believe -- if we can deal with information which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It's not a problem, Your Honour. I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- based on things that he actually knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: After you learned that your wife and children were in Srebrenica, what did you do? Did you take any steps with respect to finding them or learning any information about them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took steps immediately. I got up and went to see my friend Milos Okanovic at Grabovac. His wife and he kept me alive. She would take me to see a doctor and help me to stay on my feet, to stay alive. The house across the way from Bjelovac, I came to see him. He's a radio technician and he's also a ham radio operator. He had been doing that for over 30 years. I came to see him and I said: A while ago I had recorded a conversation and then I erased it, and he said: Well, yes, I heard the same conversation. That Naser called personally and said they were with him in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Naser who? Did you have a last name? Did he tell you? Who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you just knew. Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you take any steps with respect to -- well, what did you do after that, after he told you that Naser Oric -- he had heard over the radio that Naser Oric had them and that they were with him? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At first, the next day, because I found out late in the evening, so the next day I went to Bratunac, to the command, and I asked to speak to the commander, to see if an exchange could be arranged. However, there was chaos there. There were no negotiations, as if it wasn't about children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And then what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I lost all hope. I went again to see my friend Milos. I tried everything. On one occasion, I overheard a conversation - those were coded conversations - a person referred to as "The Lion." He said Naser was reporting regularly and his code-name was "Boss." So this person said: Do you have anything to exchange? And he said, the boss said: Yes. I have all the persons for the exchange, with the exception of the women from Bjelovac. And that was when I lost hope. I couldn't understand why, why it was them precisely that were not to be exchanged. So I was looking for something to do, something that I could do, and I came to see this friend again. I would listen to these radio communications to see if I could hear something that was important. At one point, Milos joined in a conversation with Naser, and he said: What sort of a commander are you? Aren't you ashamed to keep these children captured? You captured a six-month-old baby. Aren't you ashamed? And he replied: Whoever is on the front line are soldiers for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just let me just stop you for a moment, Mr. Filipovic. Who were you and Milos listening to? You were listening to the radio, and you were overhearing conversations, and could you tell us who the conversations -- what were the voices, and who was part of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Shouldn't he be asked if he recognised any of the voices?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can get to that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's jumping the gun a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can proceed along the lines of this question and we'll see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies. Please proceed with your question and then we'll take care of what you have raised. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The conversations that you and Milos were listening to, who were those conversations between? Who were having those conversations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Naser Oric and a person with the code-name "Lion." I'm not sure who this person was. It was probably someone from Vlasenica, since they also had their own detainees, and that's who this person was asking about. And then he said that they were all to be exchanged, only the women and children from Bjelovac were not to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And after he said that, what happened next? What was the next thing that you heard on the radio?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I've lost focus a little now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you need a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll have a break --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- instead of a few minutes. We are going to have a 25-minute break starting from now. Basically, we will resume at 5.00, in other words -- at 6.00, sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Filipovic. If you see that you are tired, if you see that you are tired and you wish us to stop for today, just let me know and we will stop whenever you tell us. I want you to give evidence in a relaxed way. I know these are not events that are easy for you to deal with. So at any time if you feel tired or losing concentration, please draw my attention and we will stop for the day and we will continue tomorrow. Don't worry about it. You will find us very understanding. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, before the break we were discussing the radio transmission, and we also -- you also testified that you were listening to the radio with your friend Milos. I would like to ask -- my question to you is: You said that you heard on the radio Naser Oric with someone by the code-name of "Lion," and that they were discussing exchanges, but not the women and children of Bjelovac. Could you tell us how you knew that this was Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the usual thing. He would spend a lot of time on the radio link every day, and his voice was a familiar one. I knew it was he, and he responded to the code-name "Boss" --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- "Gazda" in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said you were familiar with his voice. What do you mean? How were you familiar with his voice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I had occasion to meet Naser previously. I had repaired his car on several occasions, around 1990. I was friendly with his father. His father built diesel engines, and we did the regular engines. So we exchanged jobs and we tried to help each other out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you worked -- you fixed Naser Oric's car, and you said on several occasions. Did you actually meet Naser Oric, had conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How long were you and Milos listening that day before you heard the comments about the women and children from Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I spent some time there every day. I was waiting to see whether any news would come my way. I can't tell exactly how long on that particular occasion. It was 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand. And do you remember what time of the day, if you know, that you actually overheard that portion of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At dusk. I recall the continuation of that conversation, or rather, our conversation. If you wish, we can pick up from there again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please tell us about that conversation that you overheard.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's how far we got. Naser talked to Milos Okanovic in the following words: You're the Serb catching all our frequencies, and then from Kunjerac some days later, his house was targeted and the house next door to his was hit. His wife, Kralja Radovic, took the kids and left. So many people in the area across the way from Bjelovac became refugees in their own area. The children stopped going to school. They stayed in a field not far from the river, in Kraljevo. The children were no longer allowed to use the road, because some people had been wounded on the other side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the conversation, could you tell us again what was said by you? Did you say anything as you were listening, after the comment was made about the women and children from Bjelovac, or did Milos say anything?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: He said: Shame on you. What sort of a commander are you? I think we've been through that. He said: You capture children. You keep children detained. And he spoke back to him, saying: Whoever happens to be on the front line, for me, is a fighter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, is this Milos still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen his name amongst the list of witnesses that the Prosecution intends to bring forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will revisit that issue, about whether or not we do intend to call him, but he is at this time not on the list. But we are -- we will revisit our list as we go along, and as witnesses come in and we get information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to -- I think it's important for us to know at this point in time whether you intend to bring this witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can give you a further update after I discuss this later with Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Because if you're intending to bring this witness, it's one way. If you don't intend to bring forward this witness or he's not available, then it's another case, and certain questions could be directed to the witness by us or by the Defence, or even by you, you know. I mean, it's ... Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, just for the sake of clarification -- just a minute here. Now, you said here he -- you said, he said: Shame on you. What sort of a commander are you? Who is this "he"? Was it Milos, your friend with whom you were listening, or was it a person who had a conversation with the said Naser Oric? Was it "Lion" saying this or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Milos. Between you and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Milos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... conversation between both of you at that place? You did not have -- Milos did not have direct conversation -- he had --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milos and Naser had a direct conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In addition, I mean, it's a follow-up, you were present during this conversation that Milos had with, according to you, Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you told us that you knew Naser Oric personally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this time, you already knew that there was no intention on the part of Naser Oric - again, I'm repeating you - to release the women and children from Bjelovac. You knew this already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you think of using your former friendship or acquaintance, whichever way you want to put it, with Naser Oric while you were next to Milos to address him personally and say: I am the husband of Mira and the little children? Did it occur to your mind? And if it did, why didn't you do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a reason why you couldn't do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I left the whole thing to the authorities and the armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Fair enough. Fair enough. Yes, Ms. Richardson. My apologies to you for having interrupted you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you listened to the radio during the day with Milos. Did you overhear any other conversations or comments by Naser Oric during that time, other than what was said about --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing further in relation to my case, and I wasn't much interested in anything else. Everyone talked over this radio link. Ham radio operators, the military, everyone took part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "everyone," are you talking about the Muslim military or the Serb military? Who are you referring to when you say "everyone"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Ham radio operators from Belgrade got involved; the Muslim and the Serb armies, people from Zvornik talked. It's a channel, a frequency they used for military and secret. It wasn't really for military and secret operations. It was more for fun that they used this frequency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, at the time you -- you testified previously that you were traumatised, and that might be my description of what your state was, but you were drinking and so on. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what your state of mind was on that particular day that you were listening to the radio? Were you -- and I should also ask: Were you drinking on that day and were you able to listen attentively to the conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was able to listen attentively. Whatever my state of mind was at the moment, this was something that very much concerned me personally, so I followed closely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, do you see the individual whose car you worked on in 1990, previously, in the courtroom sitting here?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we're going to have a dock ID, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even a 2-year-old boy wouldn't miss the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that your wife and children were in fact exchanged or released from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The 16th of February, at Skelani. That's where the exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You earlier testified, Mr. Filipovic, that you were a member of the village guard. Did there come a time that you were mobilised by the Serb military in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received a call-up, whether it was late April or early May. They did send call-ups, but no one responded from our village. We were all just there. I'm not sure what the wording was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you didn't report to the Serb military for training?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you didn't receive any weapons or uniforms from them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You testified earlier that you were no longer working in the mine in April of 1992. Were you -- how were you supporting your family?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We had some stocks, some supplies. We had a little money. I was from a family that was rather well off, so this was not a problem. We had enough to last us the war. Later on, the Red Cross came in too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during that period of time, did you receive monies from any authority?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Some money was distributed. I'm not sure about the establishments. Those drivers working in the mines, the mine -- the supplies in the mines were being sold. It passed through the military. So several times, money was distributed to people, but I don't know how many times or how much money exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you ever paid by the Serb military in 1992 prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No one spoke to us. No one came to us. I don't know, the money, where would it have come from. I see a list and I see that it's not my signature or my father's. I'm not sure who brought it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But as far as you know, you were not paid by the Serb military. No one -- you're not aware of being paid by the Serb military.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure who paid the money, whether it was the military or someone else. I know it was from the mine, the money from the mine that was being distributed. Whether it was done through the military or in a different way, there was a little money. But the amounts were not large.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you became an active member of the Serb military following the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Following the attack?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: After the attack in your village, did you become a member of the Serb military then, after 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I became one much later, after the attack. I was a member of the TO and I had a work duty. I drove water to Bratunac. I could no longer go there. They asked me to do something for them, so I drove -- I transported water. That was my work assignment. You go as far as the line. It was all the same army, although I did have a lot of trouble with the military police. They'd come to pick me up, but I refused to go. And at one point in time, for five or six months, I was in the military records. I think in late 1993 or the 14th of February, 1994, I left the military, and there was no way they could make me go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, are you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did enrol when the SDS was established, at the beginning, but I was never an active member, and I'm not on good terms with them anyway, with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall paying membership dues or attending the meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't pay any membership dues, ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you returned to your village following the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In February, when it was liberated, five or six days later, I came to the village and spent some two hours there. And then I went back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Why did you return in February? Were you unable to return sooner?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was driving this cistern with the water, and so I had to go back. But I couldn't actually go back until 2002, because everything was destroyed. So where could I go back to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, after the attack on the 14th, and I believe you testified earlier that on the 15th there was no one in the village, do you know if the village was under Muslim forces or was it under the Serb forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the 15th, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th, everybody was thrown out, expelled, all our people, all our forces were expelled, the civilians, the army, the army that had come in as reinforcements. They all crossed the Drina River at night. In February, I don't know the exact date that Bjelovac was liberated, but there was nobody else left there. Whether the Muslims were there, whether they were soldiers or civilians, I don't know. I wasn't there. I don't know who was there. But they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like to at this time ask the usher to assist with handing out some photographs we will be using with this witness. And it's on Sanction. If we could have a Prosecution exhibit number assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could we be told when these pictures were taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have a witness that will be coming in as we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- using these photographs through crime-base witnesses. But a professional photographer who actually took these pictures - date, time, and circumstances, and under the circumstances the pictures were taken - will be testifying shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, if the photos are being made use of during the testimony of this witness, which will soon be followed by the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the photos were taken in 19 -- I believe 1993 or 1994. I'm sorry, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It must be possible to get the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We do have the precise dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, yes, please, if you could find that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It should be available.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We're doing that as we speak, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start with giving the photos an exhibit number. First of all, how many of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fifteen?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And this will be Prosecution Exhibit P452? 452. And P452 consists of 15 photos marked sequentially from 0108-8029 to 0108-8043, both numbers included.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As we're waiting for confirmation of the date, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, we can start.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you testified earlier that you returned to your village in February of 1993. Did you have an opportunity to observe some of the homes, the houses in the village, and observe the conditions of the homes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was burnt was burnt. The rest was destroyed. Roofs taken off, all the woodwork taken away.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: I would ask you to take a look at your monitor, or -- and tell us if you recognise Prosecution Exhibit 452, ERN number 8029. Do you recognise that house, that structure?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, the right-hand half, was the cafe belonging to Drasko Sekaric, and the left-hand side, the left part of the house was a family home, a family house. And on the right was also a business premises, as I said, belonging to Drasko Sekaric.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Now, when you returned in February, was this one of the structures that you were able -- that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And does this -- the picture accurately reflect how it appeared to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The next photograph, 8030.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Could you take a look at that building and tell us if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's the health centre in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And was this one of the buildings you saw in February?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And does this -- the picture appear as -- does the picture accurately reflect how this building appeared on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Next photograph, 8031. Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The same thing. It's the cafe belonging to Nedeljko Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And is this how it appeared when you saw it in February? If there's anything different, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there probably is some difference. In February, I passed by. This photograph was taken later on. The grass is taller here. I passed by in February. And I can see that the grass growing out of the roof or walls is higher than it was.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: But does the building itself appear like you saw it in February?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that they had been burnt down -- well, I didn't focus on any differences. I wasn't interested in looking at the differences and scrutinising each individual house. I just went back through the village. I went back and saw that the village had been burnt down. As to the damage and type of damage and extent of damage, I wasn't in any expert commission to establish damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I find something very artificial in this exercise, in that unless Mr. Filipovic either took these photographs or somewhere recorded which houses he saw in February 1993, one is left with this rather strange coincidence that every single one of these pictures is a house which he went and had a look at in February 1993. It may be a point for cross-examination, but surely for an accurate record, one should first of all ask Mr. Filipovic, Which houses did you see in February 1993, without any photographic aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the first question should be: Do you recognise this house or the remains of this house and move from there --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it would also be practical and move ahead, and at the end of the day --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because we're prompting this witness to recall seeing these houses in February 1993, which there's no reason to suppose he went and looked at every single one of the houses that was photographed. It's a very artificial exercise, and that's all I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would say: Do you recognise this building or the remains of this house?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can continue along that line. That's fine. The witness seems to be answering for himself who's building this is and so it's precluding me from asking that very question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, it's not important. I mean, it's not going to change anything at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Please look at the next photograph, 8032. Do you recognise this house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I know who the old owner is, two brothers, Djokanovic, and this is Milivoj Djokanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever see this house in this condition, as shown in this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't be sure. I know -- I recognise the house. I know the house. Now, this state, well, I passed by, saw the village had been burnt. Now, what state this house was in, I really can't say. The elements added to the damage, because the rain and everything else --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is -- the witness said "I don't know," and here it says "I'm not sure." The -- I would like to ask the interpreters to take care when they're translating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Did you say you're not sure or did you say "I don't know"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean whose house this is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Not whose house it is. Whether you had ever seen it in this condition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that the village had been burnt. Now, whether I saw it in this actual condition, I went past the village, I spent two hours there. I was more interested in reaching my own house rather than scrutinising the other houses. I saw that it had burnt, been burnt. Now, in assessing the extent of the damage, well, I really can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when would this be? Which month and which year that you could have possibly seen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I went in the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You see, if you move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The first time. That is, in which month and which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] February 1993. It was -- there was snow in the village when I entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think if you move along these lines, we will get there quicker.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: If you take a look at that photograph. And could -- do you recognise that house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Vladimir Djokanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And is this the condition of the house when you went through the village on February 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that it had been set on fire. Now, whether it looked like this, the nuances, I don't know, but I remember it being roughly like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can just identify the house and say that's the house. I can't say what it looked like in February, what it looks like now and make the comparison.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: That's fine. Do you recognise the owner of this house? Whose house is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Rankic. Tomo and Radoj was the next house.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next photograph. 8035.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat that answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please. Whose house is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Ivko Ilic's.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And based on your memory, does this look anything like it did when you went through the village in February? If you don't recall, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Okay. 8036, do you know --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Radovan Jovanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And do you recall going by this house, and does this picture appear as it did then? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I walked past that area. I walked past them all. I have to keep repeating that I wasn't interested in noticing things like that. I wanted to see what my house was like in February, or what it looked like when these photos were taken. The village had been set fire to, so what had burnt down had burnt down.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. For the next series of photographs we would just ask you if you identify it and then we will move on. So next photograph, 8037, do you recognise that house and who it belongs to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The community centre.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Bozana Jovanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mihajlovic Srecko's house. Srecko Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Bozana Damjanovic's.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Spomenka Vucetic's house.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My house.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Now, in February -- you saw your house in February. Did your house appear similar to this picture?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there weren't more damages. A little bit of the roof remained standing so that the walls were protected.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Okay. And the next photograph, 8043, do you recognise this house? It's a bit of a distance, but can you tell whose house this is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Radojka Damjanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Now, did anyone -- did you receive compensation from the Bosnian Muslim army for damage to your home?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just -- this question is always requested and I've objected to it once. I won't insist on objecting to it. But firstly it presumes that the Bosnian Muslim army was responsible, which is an issue in trial. But secondly, we come back to the point that what is the Bosnian Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You ask me? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely. What does that even mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day, it's a question of evidence and proof, Mr. Jones, as you know. I have a question for you, sir. You have seen here 15 photos of houses. Each photo shows a house. And each house seems to be either destroyed or seriously damaged. When you visited the village in February of 1993, were any of the houses that you have seen in these photos in one piece, undamaged or undestroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In fact, I do not. However, I do have that information with respect to the date of the photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The photos, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The photos were taken sometime between 8 July 1994 and August 1994. Again, it's a project. The photographer will be coming in to give testimony about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at least we know that they had seen two winters, I mean, and two summers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have 15 minutes, Madam Vidovic. Do you want to start now or do you want to start tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to begin tomorrow, with the Court's indulgence, because I would like to look through the box and then be allowed to begin tomorrow, if that is at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll give you a rest, Mr. Filipovic. We'll let you go back to your hotel. You will return to the courtroom, to this Tribunal, tomorrow in the afternoon, same time like today, and we will start, hopefully, at a quarter past 2.00 and try to finish with you tomorrow. I want to make sure that between today and tomorrow, you will not contact or discuss the matters of your evidence and these events with anyone, neither members of the Prosecution nor other witnesses that may have come from your area, absolutely no one. And if anyone approaches you, tomorrow afternoon, first thing, you need to tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That also includes telephone calls that you may make or receive from persons in your own country or persons -- other persons elsewhere. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So the sitting stands adjourned until tomorrow at 2.15, Courtroom I. Thank you.
